idiom_name: sealed interface Node + data classes + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Kotlin's sealed interfaces and classes with the when expression replace the GoF hierarchy: all direct subclasses are known at compile time, so a when over the node type is checked exhaustively and needs no else branch (kotlinlang.org). Node kinds become data classes (or data objects for parameterless cases) and each operation is a recursive top-level function, which keeps behaviour outside the data - the opposite trade to adding a method to every node. Prefer it when the node set is closed and owned by one module; switch to the open-hierarchy variant when other modules must contribute node kinds, since sealed subclasses must share the parent's package and module.
pitfalls: Publishing a sealed type makes a new node kind a breaking change: every exhaustive when in every consuming module stops compiling (that is the guarantee, but it must be planned for).
Sealed direct subclasses must live in the same package and module as the parent, which constrains multi-module layouts.
data class equality is structural, so two identical containers compare equal and collections do not distinguish them.

variants.name: Open interface with a mutable child list (extensible node set)
variants.idiom_name: interface Node + MutableList children, child management on the container
variants.implementation_notes: The direct Kotlin translation of the classic form: an interface (or abstract class) declares the uniform operation, leaves implement it, and a container class keeps a MutableList<Node> and delegates recursively. This is the shape to choose when node kinds are open to other modules, when nodes are stateful and identity matters, or when the tree is edited in place - none of which a sealed hierarchy supports. Child management stays on the container class so leaves do not inherit meaningless add/remove members.
pitfalls: Exposing the MutableList lets callers corrupt the tree; publish a read-only view and mutate only through validated methods.
Nothing prevents a parent/child cycle in an open hierarchy, and a cycle turns traversal into infinite recursion.
Each operation is overridden per node class, so a new operation touches every class - the classic expression-problem trade-off.
